title: Sickle Cell Vaso-Occlusive Crisis
scenario: A 19-year-old male with sickle cell disease (HbSS) presents to the emergency department with severe diffuse bone pain in his back, arms, and legs that began yesterday after a soccer match in hot weather. He rates the pain 9 out of 10.

lines: 19-year-old male with known sickle cell disease (HbSS) presents with severe generalized bone and joint pain rated 9/10, worst in the lumbar spine and long bones. Reports last crisis 4 months ago. States he ran out of hydroxyurea 2 weeks ago and had limited fluids during a soccer tournament in the heat. Mucous membranes dry. Alert and oriented x3. Guarding and grimacing with movement.
IV access obtained in the right forearm. Labs drawn and sent. Oxygen applied at 2L per nasal cannula. Cardiac and pulse-oximetry monitoring initiated. Provider at bedside.
IV morphine administered per order. Isotonic IV fluids infusing. Warm compresses applied to affected limbs. Repositioned for comfort.
Reports pain now 3/10 and is resting more comfortably. Voiding clear yellow urine. Mucous membranes moist. Ambulated to bathroom with steady gait.
Hydroxyurea 1000 mg PO daily (reports not taken for 2 weeks)
Morphine 4 mg IV every 2 hours PRN severe pain
Oxygen to maintain SpO2 greater than 94%
Incentive spirometer every hour while awake
Notify provider for temperature above 101 F or worsening hypoxia

children.subject: Medical-Surgical
children.rationale: Uncontrolled severe pain, hypoxia, tachycardia, and dehydration all drive and reflect sickling and require prompt intervention. Normal orientation and a mildly elevated temperature are not immediate priorities.

children.subject: Medical-Surgical
children.stem: For each finding, click to specify whether it reflects hemolysis, vaso-occlusion, or both. Each finding may reflect more than one.
children.rationale: Elevated bilirubin and reticulocytosis reflect red cell breakdown (hemolysis). Bone pain reflects tissue ischemia from vaso-occlusion. Low hemoglobin with high LDH results from both chronic hemolysis and ongoing sickling.

children.subject: Medical-Surgical
children.stem: Complete the sentence. The nurse determines that the priority problem is {1}, and the priority initial intervention is {2}.

choices.text: acute pain with impaired tissue perfusion

children.rationale: The immediate threat in vaso-occlusive crisis is severe pain from tissue ischemia; aggressive analgesia and hydration to reduce sickling take priority over other real but less urgent concerns.

children.subject: Medical-Surgical
children.stem: For each intervention, click to specify whether it is indicated or contraindicated for this client.

rows.text: Apply warm compresses to painful areas
Apply cold packs to painful joints

children.rationale: Hydration, warmth, and oxygen reduce sickling and relieve ischemic pain. Cold causes vasoconstriction that worsens sickling, and fluid restriction promotes dehydration and further sickling.

children.subject: Medical-Surgical
children.stem: Which actions should the nurse take to manage this client's crisis? Select all that apply.

options.text: Administer IV morphine on a scheduled/PRN basis
Encourage use of the incentive spirometer
Titrate oxygen to keep SpO2 above 94%
Apply ice packs to the painful limbs

children.rationale: Opioid analgesia, hydration, oxygenation, and incentive spirometry (to prevent acute chest syndrome) are standard crisis care. Withholding opioids and applying cold are inappropriate and worsen outcomes.

children.subject: Medical-Surgical
children.stem: Which findings indicate the treatment has been effective? Select all that apply.

options.text: Mucous membranes now moist with clear urine output

children.rationale: Reduced pain, improved oxygenation, a normalizing heart rate, and restored hydration all show the crisis is resolving. A rising respiratory rate would suggest a worsening respiratory complication, not improvement.
